```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# Every chunk on this page runs from the folder of the case, so that the paths
# read exactly as they do in the workspace and in the browser lab:
# data/housing_audit.csv.
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = "../cases/housing")
```

```{r}
#| label: page-numbers
#| include: false
# The numbers quoted in the prose, computed from the files of the course.
fmt <- \(x, d = 1) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d) |> sub(pattern = "^-", replacement = "−")

page_audit <- readr::read_csv("data/housing_audit.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
page_curve <- readr::read_csv("data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

n_emails    <- nrow(page_audit)
n_bounced   <- sum(is.na(page_audit$reply))
n_delivered <- sum(!is.na(page_audit$reply))
n_replies   <- sum(page_audit$reply %in% 1)
n_coded     <- sum(!is.na(page_audit$named))

share_of <- \(rows, g) 100 * mean(rows$y[rows$group == g])
replies_wh <- page_audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named), group %in% c("white", "hispanic")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(y = named)
delivered_wh <- page_audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(reply), group %in% c("white", "hispanic")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(y = dplyr::if_else(reply == 1, named, 0)) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(y))
white_share <- share_of(replies_wh, "white")
hisp_share  <- share_of(replies_wh, "hispanic")
gap_replies <- hisp_share - white_share
gap_all     <- share_of(delivered_wh, "hispanic") - share_of(delivered_wh, "white")
ref_row     <- page_curve |> datawizard::data_filter(is_reference)
published   <- readr::read_csv("data/reference_marks.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(id == "OA")
```

This is the first module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd), and it is written for the person who arrives with no R at all: a student, a professional from another field, or anyone curious about how the analysis of the course is built. It does not assume that you have programmed before. Sections 1 to 13 work on one file, the housing-audit data, which holds one row for each of the `r format(n_emails, big.mark = ",")` emails that the original authors (OAs) sent to public housing authorities in the United States, signed with names meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic applicant [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]. The [case study](../cases/housing/index.qmd) tells the story of the experiment. Here it serves as a dataset small enough to look at whole, with an outcome that is either yes or no, which makes it a good place to learn. By the end you will be able to read the file into R, look at it, reshape it with a handful of verbs, compute the share of replies that greeted the sender by name and the difference between two such shares, set the result out as a table and as a figure, and fit your first specification with the helper that the exercise uses.

Sections 14 to 16 take the same tools further, for a second reading, and they stay with the emails. Section 14 reads the Stata file that the OAs deposited, with its labels, and introduces the packages that fetch data from an archive. Section 15 sets out the three dialects in which R is written, and section 16 the habit of naming the estimand before a model is read.

Unlike many pages that teach R, this one runs its code. The blocks were executed when the page was built, and what R printed appears underneath each of them, so you can compare your own output with the page line by line. The way to learn is still to type. Copy each block into the workspace that you downloaded from the [setup page](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/setup.html), or into the [browser lab](../cases/housing/lab.qmd), where a copy of R starts inside the browser tab with the data already in place.

The courses use the module at several points. It is the companion of the R tutorial in Part 2 of the [one-day course on data tools](../tracks/housing-one-day-data-tools/part-2.qmd), which works on the same emails, and optional preparation for the [one-day course with a methods focus](../tracks/housing-one-day-methods/before.qmd). The self-study track reads sections 1 to 5 in [stage 1](../tracks/self-study/stage-1.qmd) and sections 6 to 13 in [stage 2](../tracks/self-study/stage-2.qmd).

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

The browser lab is the quickest way to follow along on a first read, since there is nothing to install. It loads the data for you as an object called `audit` and has datawizard, dplyr, tinyplot and parameters ready, but it does not hold readr, tinytable, ggplot2, haven, performance or modelbased. Skip the line that reads the file in [section 6](#sec-reading), the formatted table in [section 11](#sec-table), the ggplot2 figures at the end of [section 12](#sec-ggplot), the Stata file of [section 14](#sec-formats) and everything in [section 16](#sec-easystats) after `parameters::model_parameters()`; everything else runs there as printed.
:::

## 1. R and the IDE {#sec-what}

**R** is a programming language built for working with data: reading it, reshaping it, fitting statistical models to it and drawing figures from it. It is free and open source, and it is one of the common languages of quantitative social science, which is why the analysis of the course is written in it. On its own, R is a program that reads instructions and returns answers.

**The IDE** is the program from which you drive R. An IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.), short for integrated development environment, is a window with your files on one side, a place to write and run code, and panels that show results, figures and the objects you have made. Newcomers often run the language and the environment together, although each is installed separately. You install R once, so that the language is on your machine, and you install an IDE once, as the place where you work. When the IDE first opens, it finds the R that you installed and connects to it. The [setup page](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/setup.html) walks through both installations, and the [IDE module](ide.qmd) sets the three common IDEs side by side, pane by pane.

## 2. The console, the script and the report {#sec-surfaces}

There are three surfaces into which you type R, and knowing which is for what saves a great deal of confusion later.

The **console** is the interactive prompt. You type one line, press Enter, and R answers immediately. It is the place to try something out, check a value or do a quick sum. Its weakness is that everything typed there is lost when the session closes, with no record of how you reached a result.

A **script** is a plain text file with the extension `.R` that holds a sequence of commands you want to keep. You write the commands in the script and send them to the console from there, all at once or line by line. A script runs the same way tomorrow and on someone else's machine, and it shows step by step how a result was produced. The course follows a simple rule: try things in the console, and move anything that matters into a script.

A **Quarto document**, with the extension `.qmd`, is a script and a written report in one file. It holds ordinary prose with blocks of R code, called chunks, between the paragraphs. When the document is rendered, R runs every chunk and places its results, whether tables, figures or numbers, into the finished report at the point where they belong. The workspace of the course holds the same exercise in both forms: `working_script.R` takes you through Tasks 1 to 5 as a plain script, and `index.qmd` is the report that you fill in and render. The [Quarto module](quarto.qmd) shows how such a document is written.

## 3. Objects and vectors {#sec-objects}

R works by putting values into named **objects** and then referring to them by name. You assign a value to a name with the arrow `<-`, typed as a less-than sign followed by a hyphen. From then on, the name stands in for the value.

```{r}
#| label: objects
emails_sent <- 1014         # a single number
first_name  <- "Santiago"   # text, called a character string, is quoted
bounced     <- FALSE        # a logical value: TRUE or FALSE

emails_sent                 # typing a name prints its value
```

Most data come as runs of values rather than single ones. A **vector** is an ordered run of values of one type, built with `c()`, for 'combine'. Arithmetic works on the whole vector at once, which is why R rarely needs the loops that other languages reach for. The two vectors below hold, for the white, the Black and the Hispanic names in turn, the number of emails that reached an official and the number of replies that came back.

```{r}
#| label: vectors
delivered <- c(308, 326, 357)   # white, Black and Hispanic names
replies   <- c(177, 198, 188)

replies / delivered             # three reply rates, in one step
sum(replies)                    # every reply
replies[3]                      # the third value: the Hispanic names
```

These six numbers were typed by hand, and [section 9](#sec-verbs) computes them from the file, which is how you would check them.

One small fact carries most of the arithmetic of the course. When a vector holds only 1s and 0s, its **mean is the share of 1s**. The outcome of the claim, whether a reply opened with the name of the sender, is stored in exactly that way, with 1 for a greeting by name and 0 for none, so the share of replies that greeted the sender by name is the mean of that column.

```{r}
#| label: share-as-mean
greeted <- c(1, 0, 1, 1, 0)   # five replies: 1 = opened with the name of the sender
mean(greeted)                 # three of the five
```

Real data also have gaps. R marks a missing value with `NA`, for 'not available', and any calculation that meets one returns `NA` in turn, because the answer cannot be known. The argument `na.rm = TRUE` tells a summary function to remove the missing values first.

```{r}
#| label: missing-values
greeted <- c(1, 0, NA, 1, 0)   # the third reply carries no greeting code
mean(greeted)
mean(greeted, na.rm = TRUE)    # the share among the four coded replies
```

The housing-audit data have missing values of three kinds, and each means something different: an email that bounced has no reply status, an email without a reply has no greeting, and `r n_replies - n_coded` replies were never coded for their greeting. Deciding what to do with each of them is part of the analysis, which is why the course never uses `na.rm = TRUE` without saying which rows it removes.

## 4. Data frames {#sec-dataframes}

A **data frame** is how R stores a table: a set of vectors of equal length standing side by side as columns, with one row per observation. Almost everything in the course is a data frame. Here is a small one built by hand, three emails with the name that signed each, whether a reply came, and whether the reply greeted the sender by name:

```{r}
#| label: data-frame
emails <- data.frame(
  name  = c("Brett", "Santiago", "Emily"),
  reply = c(1, 1, 0),
  named = c(1, 0, NA)
)

emails
```

Base R, the core that ships with R itself, reaches into a data frame with two operators. The `$` sign pulls out one column as a vector, and square brackets take a block by `[rows, columns]`, where an empty slot means 'all of them'.

```{r}
#| label: base-access
emails$named   # one column, as a vector
emails[1:2, ]  # the first two rows, every column
```

You will meet both in code that other people write, and `$` is often the quickest way to look at a single column. For reshaping a table, the course uses the verbs of [section 9](#sec-verbs), which say in words what each step does. The emails without a reply show why the third value of `named` is missing: no reply, so no greeting to code.

## 5. Packages {#sec-packages}

Everything so far, from `c()` to `mean()` and `data.frame()`, comes with R itself. Everything else arrives as **packages**: bundles of functions and their documentation, written by researchers and developers and published on CRAN, the Comprehensive R Archive Network, which holds more than twenty thousand of them. The function that reads a CSV file in the next section, `read_csv()`, comes from a package called readr, and the sections after it lean on packages for nearly everything.

Using a package takes two steps, and the difference between them trips nearly every newcomer at least once. The block below is shown and not run, because installing is something that you do once on your own machine.

```{r}
#| label: packages
#| eval: false
install.packages("pak")   # once on a new machine: the installer of the course # r-style: keep – the one-off bootstrap of pak
pak::pak("readr")         # step 1: download a package to your machine – once
readr::read_csv("data/housing_audit.csv")   # step 2: call a function by its package and its name
```

`pak::pak()` downloads a package, together with everything that it depends on, and stores it on your machine. You run it once, and again only when you want an update. The second step is the call itself, and the course writes every function that does not come with R by the name of its package, two colons and the name of the function, as in `readr::read_csv()`. Written that way, a line works in any session on a machine where the package is installed, and anyone who reads it can see at once where each function comes from, which matters when two packages offer functions of the same name. You will also meet the older habit of attaching a package to the session with `library(readr)` at the top of a script, after which its functions can be called by their names alone. The two error messages that you will meet most often come from these two steps: `there is no package called 'readr'` means that step 1 never happened on this machine, and `could not find function "read_csv"` means that the function was called by its name alone in a session to which its package was never attached.

Research code that only its authors run, such as the scripts of a paper, is often written the other way, with every function called by its name alone, and the facilitator of the course writes it so. What keeps it readable is a single import script, run at the top of every other script of the project, that attaches each package with `library()` and lists in `include.only` the functions that the project takes from it. Anyone who wants to know where a function comes from then has one place to look. Two attached packages can offer functions of the same name, and the conflicted package stops with an error when such a name is called, until `conflicts_prefer()` has said which of the two is meant:

```{r}
#| label: import-script
#| eval: false
# R/00_packages.R: the packages of a project and the functions taken from each
library(readr, include.only = c("read_csv", "write_csv"))
library(datawizard, include.only = c("data_filter", "data_summary", "data_tabulate"))
library(dplyr, include.only = c("filter", "if_else"))
library(conflicted)
conflicts_prefer(dplyr::filter)   # stats::filter(), which R attaches at start-up, has the same name
```

The course writes `pkg::fun()` in all of its own code because that code is read a block at a time, by people who did not write it, and each block has to say where its functions come from without an import script beside it.

In the workspace, `R/check_setup.R` checks the twelve packages that the exercise needs (dplyr, purrr, readr, tibble, datawizard, parameters, sandwich, marginaleffects, effectsize, tinyplot, dagitty and rmarkdown) and, if any are missing, prints the line that installs them.

## 6. Reading the data {#sec-reading}

You will rarely type data by hand. Most data arrive as a **CSV** file, short for 'comma-separated values': a plain text table in which each line is a row and commas divide the columns. The course ships its data this way because any program can open a CSV, and because version control can compare two versions of it line by line. `read_csv()` from readr reads one into a data frame:

```{r}
#| label: read-data
audit <- readr::read_csv("data/housing_audit.csv")
```

The message that follows the call reports how many rows and columns were read and which type readr inferred for each column: `chr` for character columns such as `name` and `group`, `dbl` for numbers. Reading that message is the first check on any import.

The path `"data/housing_audit.csv"` is written relative to the folder of the workspace, not as `C:/Users/yourname/Desktop/...`. A relative path works on any machine that holds the project, and an absolute path breaks as soon as the work moves. Open the workspace folder in your IDE, and every path in the course works as written.

Typing the name prints the data frame. readr returns a **tibble**, a data frame that prints its size, the type of each column and only the first ten rows, so that a large table does not flood the console:

```{r}
#| label: print-data
audit
nrow(audit)    # how many rows
names(audit)   # the names of the columns
```

The workspace also holds `audit_original.csv`, the public file of the OAs with their own column names, on which the reproduction of Task 3 runs. Both files are described column by column in their codebooks, [`housing_audit_codebook.md`](../cases/housing/data/housing_audit_codebook.md) and [`audit_original_codebook.md`](../cases/housing/data/audit_original_codebook.md), and a codebook is the second thing to read after any import.

Data reach researchers in other formats too. The OAs deposited their file on the Harvard Dataverse in the format of Stata, a statistical package, and the course converted it to CSV; the [data sources module](data-sources.qmd#sec-dataverse) shows how to download the deposited file. The haven package reads Stata (`read_dta()`) and SPSS (`read_sav()`) files with their labels, readxl reads Excel workbooks one sheet at a time, and arrow reads the newer Parquet format, which stores the type of each column inside the file. Whatever the source, the result is the same kind of data frame, and everything below applies to it unchanged. [Section 14](#sec-formats) reads the deposited Stata file and introduces the packages that fetch data straight from an archive.

## 7. Looking at the data {#sec-looking}

Before any analysis, look at what you have. The first question to ask of any dataset is what a row is, and here a row is one email. `data_peek()` from datawizard, the package of [section 9](#sec-verbs), turns the table on its side, with one line per column, its type and its first values, which fits all sixteen columns on one screen:

```{r}
#| label: glimpse
datawizard::data_peek(audit)
```

`data_tabulate()` counts the rows for each value of a column and gives each count as a percentage. It answers the first questions about an experiment, how many emails each group of names received and how many of them drew a reply:

```{r}
#| label: count-group
datawizard::data_tabulate(audit, select = "group")
datawizard::data_tabulate(audit, select = "reply")
```

The `NA` in the second table is the `r n_bounced` emails that bounced and never reached an official, and the column of valid percentages leaves them out. Tabulating one column by another shows how the outcome depends on the reply:

```{r}
#| label: count-two
datawizard::data_tabulate(audit, select = "named", by = "reply")
```

Read the table one column at a time, since together the columns explain every missing value in the outcome. An email without a reply (the column headed 0) has no greeting, so `named` is missing. A reply (the column headed 1) carries a greeting code of 1 or 0, except for `r n_replies - n_coded` replies that nobody coded. A bounced email (the column headed `NA`) has neither. These are the counts that every analysis of the course starts from: `r format(n_emails, big.mark = ",")` emails, `r n_bounced` bounced, `r n_delivered` delivered, `r n_replies` replies and `r n_coded` replies with a greeting code.

Your IDE can also show the data as a spreadsheet. `View(audit)` opens the data viewer, where you can sort and filter the rows by clicking. Filters in the viewer change only what you are looking at and leave the data frame in your session as it was, so they are a way of looking, not of analysing.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Run `datawizard::data_tabulate(audit, select = "name", by = "group")` and check that the six names fall into the three groups as the case study says. Then run `datawizard::data_tabulate(audit, select = "reply", by = "hard_email")`: the column `hard_email` is 1 where the address of the authority could not be found quickly on its own website and was taken from the list of housing authorities kept by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). Did the harder addresses reply less often? You can answer that by eye from the counts, and section 9 shows how to compute it.
:::

## 8. The pipe {#sec-pipe}

Most of the work after reading data is reshaping it, and reshaping is almost always a sequence of steps. The **pipe**, written `|>`, exists to make such sequences readable. It takes whatever stands on its left and passes it as the first argument to the function on its right, so that instead of wrapping functions inside one another and reading them from the inside out, you write the steps from top to bottom in the order in which they happen:

```{r}
#| label: pipe
# without the pipe: read from the innermost function outwards
round(mean(audit$reply, na.rm = TRUE), 3) # r-style: keep – shown for comparison

# with the pipe: read from left to right, in the order of the steps
audit$reply |> mean(na.rm = TRUE) |> round(3)
```

Both lines give the share of delivered emails that drew a reply. On one short line the gain is small, but it grows with every step of the chains in the next section, which is why nearly all modern R is written this way. You will also meet an older pipe, `%>%`, from a package called magrittr, in code written before 2021, when the native `|>` became part of R. Read the two in the same way, and write `|>`, as all the materials of the course do.

## 9. The datawizard verbs {#sec-verbs}

The datawizard package, one of the easystats packages of [section 15](#sec-dialects), gives each common operation on a table a named verb. Each takes a data frame as its first argument and returns a data frame, which is what lets the verbs be chained with the pipe:

- `data_filter()` keeps the rows that meet a condition;
- `data_select()` keeps the columns that you name;
- `data_modify()` adds a column or changes one;
- `data_summary()` collapses many rows into one row of summaries, and with `by` into one row per group;
- `data_tabulate()` counts rows, as section 7 showed.

The dplyr package of the tidyverse has a verb for each of these, `filter()`, `select()`, `mutate()`, `summarise()` and `count()`, and you will meet them in code written by others and in a few places in the code of the course, where datawizard has no verb for the job. The course uses datawizard first, so that one family of packages covers the data work and the reading of models.

**`data_filter()`** takes a condition, and the operators of a condition are worth learning together: `==` for 'equals' (two signs, because one sign assigns), `!=` for 'does not equal', `>` and `<`, `%in%` for 'is one of', `!` for 'not', and `&` for 'and'. `is.na()` asks whether a value is missing, so `!is.na(reply)` keeps the emails that have a reply status, the delivered ones:

```{r}
#| label: filter
audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(reply)) |>
  datawizard::data_tabulate(select = "group")
```

**`data_select()`** narrows the table to the columns that matter for the task in hand, which makes it easier to read. The names of the columns go in quotes, inside `c()`:

```{r}
#| label: select
audit |>
  datawizard::data_select(select = c("name", "group", "reply", "named"))
```

**`data_modify()`** makes a new column from existing ones. The comparison `group == "hispanic"` is TRUE for the emails signed with Hispanic names and FALSE for the rest, and storing it as a column lets you count it:

```{r}
#| label: mutate
audit |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hispanic_name = group == "hispanic") |>
  datawizard::data_tabulate(select = "hispanic_name")
```

**`data_summary()`** with `by` answers 'what is this for each group?'. Inside it, `n()` counts the rows of a group, and `sum()` and `mean()` work as they did on a vector. The chain below keeps the delivered emails and reports, for each group of names, the delivered emails, the replies and the reply rate, which are the numbers typed by hand in [section 3](#sec-objects):

```{r}
#| label: group-summarise
audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(reply)) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(
    delivered  = n(),
    replies    = sum(reply),
    reply_rate = mean(reply),
    by = "group"
  )
```

Read the chain aloud and it is almost English: take the emails, keep the delivered ones, and for each group of names report three numbers. A reviewer who can read the code can check it, which is why the scripts of the course are written in these verbs. `data_summary()` sorts the groups alphabetically, and it prints the reply rates to two decimals while keeping every digit in the table that it returns, so a rate rounds only when you round it, as section 11 does.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Rewrite the chain above so that it summarises by `name` instead of `group` (`by = "name"`), and find the name that drew the fewest replies. Then summarise by `hard_email` and answer the question left open at the end of section 7.
:::

## 10. A share and a difference in shares {#sec-shares}

The claim of the case is that replies to emails signed with Hispanic names were less likely to greet the sender by name than replies to emails signed with white names. In the terms of [section 3](#sec-objects), that is a comparison of two means of a 0/1 column, so you already have the tools for it. Keep the replies that carry a greeting code, keep the white and the Hispanic names, and summarise the column `named` in each group:

```{r}
#| label: shares
shares <- audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named), group %in% c("white", "hispanic")) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(
    replies = n(),
    greeted = sum(named),
    share   = mean(named),
    by = "group"
  )

shares
```

`r fmt(white_share)`% of the replies to white names opened with the name of the sender, against `r fmt(hisp_share)`% of the replies to Hispanic names. The difference between the two shares is the estimate that the course starts from. Inside `data_summary()`, square brackets pick out the value of one group, and multiplying by 100 turns a difference in shares into a difference in percentage points:

```{r}
#| label: gap
shares |>
  datawizard::data_summary(gap_points = 100 * (share[group == "hispanic"] - share[group == "white"]))
```

A gap of `r fmt(gap_replies, 2)` points is the raw difference behind the shares that the paper reports, 61% against 41% (p. 18), and it is the **reference specification** of the course, the analysis against which every alternative on the [specification menu](../cases/housing/menu.qmd) is compared. The published estimate of `r fmt(published$b_pp)` points comes from a different calculation, a logistic regression with covariates, which the [binary-outcomes module](binary-outcomes.qmd) fits step by step, and the two agree closely.

That gap is counted among the replies only. An email that drew no reply has no greeting, so it plays no part in the calculation. The other way to count is to keep every delivered email and treat a missing reply as a reply without a greeting by name. `if_else()` from dplyr makes that column inside `data_modify()`: where `reply` is 1 it keeps the greeting code, and elsewhere it puts 0. The five uncoded replies are still missing afterwards and are filtered out.

```{r}
#| label: shares-delivered
audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(reply), group %in% c("white", "hispanic")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(greeted = dplyr::if_else(reply == 1, named, 0)) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(greeted)) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(emails = n(), share = mean(greeted), by = "group")
```

Counted this way, the gap is `r fmt(gap_all, 2)` points. The two numbers answer two questions. Among the replies, the comparison asks whether officials who answered wrote differently to the two groups of names. Among all delivered emails, it asks whether the name changed the chance of receiving a reply that greeted the sender by name at all, which mixes the decision to reply with the tone of the reply. Which emails are counted is the second argument of `try_spec()` in Task 4, and of all the decisions on the menu it is the one that moves the estimate furthest. The [causal-graphs module](dags.qmd#sec-collider) explains why the comparison among replies needs care, and the [audit-experiments module](experiments.qmd#sec-posttreatment) works through what each comparison assumes.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Compute the same gap between the Black and the white names, among the coded replies. Then compute it between two single names, Santiago and Brett, by filtering on `name` instead of `group`. The case study compares the six names, and a gap between two names is a smaller sample than a gap between two groups, so expect it to move.
:::

## 11. A first table {#sec-table}

A summary built with datawizard is already a table, and printing it in the console is enough while you work. For a report, the numbers need readable column names, sensible rounding and a caption. The chain below builds one row per group of names with the five counts that the case rests on and two percentages:

```{r}
#| label: by-group
by_group <- audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(reply)) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(
    delivered = n(),
    replies   = sum(reply),
    coded     = sum(!is.na(named)),
    greeted   = sum(named, na.rm = TRUE),
    by = "group"
  ) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(
    reply_pct   = 100 * replies / delivered,
    greeted_pct = 100 * greeted / coded
  ) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange("-greeted_pct")

by_group
```

`sum(!is.na(named))` counts the replies that carry a greeting code, because each TRUE counts as 1. `data_arrange("-greeted_pct")` sorts the rows from the largest share of greetings to the smallest, the minus sign asking for the descending order. The tinytable package then sets the same numbers out as a table for a report. `transmute()` from dplyr renames and rounds the columns in one step, keeping only the ones that it names, which no single verb of datawizard does, and `tt()` draws the table. The caption and the label beginning `tbl-` are chunk options, which the [Quarto module](quarto.qmd#sec-crossref) explains; they give the table a number that the prose can refer to, as in @tbl-groups.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-groups
#| tbl-cap: "Replies and greetings by name, by the group that the names were meant to indicate. Greetings are counted among the replies that carry a greeting code. Source: `cases/housing/data/housing_audit.csv`."
by_group |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Names                 = c(white = "White", black = "Black", hispanic = "Hispanic")[group],
    Delivered             = delivered,
    Replies               = replies,
    `Replied (%)`         = round(reply_pct, 1),
    `Greeted by name (%)` = round(greeted_pct, 1)
  ) |>
  tinytable::tt()
```

tinytable is not among the twelve packages of the workspace, so install it with `pak::pak("tinytable")` before you try this. The names in backticks, such as `` `Replied (%)` ``, are column names that contain spaces or symbols, which R accepts only inside backticks.

Task 3 meets a different kind of table. Of the five analyses that you can choose to reproduce there, the one by analyst 8PTRZ cross-tabulates two columns with the base function `xtabs()` and passes the table to a chi-square test. A first look at such a table is `datawizard::data_tabulate(audit, select = "named", by = "group")`, which holds the counts of the three groups and the missing codes beside them.

## 12. A first figure {#sec-ggplot}

Two packages draw the figures of the course. tinyplot draws every figure that you make yourself, in the workspace and in the browser lab, and ggplot2 draws the figures of the pages and slides of this site. Both describe a chart by the same few decisions: which column goes on which axis, which column sets the colour, and what kind of mark is drawn. The figures below show the share of replies that greeted the sender by name for each of the six names, first with tinyplot and then with ggplot2. First the data, one row per name:

```{r}
#| label: by-name
by_name <- audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named)) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(share = 100 * mean(named), replies = n(), by = c("group", "name"))

by_name
```

### tinyplot {#sec-tinyplot}

tinyplot extends the graphics system that comes with R itself and needs no other package, which is why it is light enough to run in the browser lab [@McDermottEtAl2026TinyplotLightweightExtension]. A plot is one call with two parts: a **formula** with the data, which says what goes on which axis, and a **type**, which says what to draw.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tinyplot-first
#| fig-cap: "The share of replies that greeted the sender by name, by name: the first draft with tinyplot."
#| fig-height: 3
tinyplot::tinyplot(share ~ name, data = by_name, type = "p", flip = TRUE)
```

The formula `share ~ name` is read 'share by name', as in a model formula: the column before the tilde goes on the vertical axis and the column after it on the horizontal one. `type = "p"` draws points, and `flip = TRUE` turns the chart on its side, so that the names are read down the vertical axis. The default look writes the labels of that axis along it, so that only some of the names fit, and the theme of the next figure sets them upright. Other types draw other marks, among them `"l"` for lines, `"s"` for the steps of a life table, `"barplot"` for bars and `"boxplot"` for boxes.

Three changes make the figure readable. A vertical bar in the formula, `share ~ name | group`, colours each mark by a third column and adds a legend that explains the colours. `type = "barplot"` draws one bar per row, with a length equal to the value in the data. And `reorder(name, share)`, applied to the data before the plot, sorts the names by the value being plotted rather than alphabetically.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tinyplot-names
#| fig-cap: "The share of replies that greeted the sender by name, by the name that signed the email, drawn with tinyplot. Source: `cases/housing/data/housing_audit.csv`."
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of six names. Emily, Brett and Tyrone lie near 60%, Shanice near 52%, Gabriela near 46% and Santiago near 37%; the bars of the two Hispanic names are burgundy."
#| fig-height: 3.4
by_name_sorted <- by_name |>
  datawizard::data_modify(name  = reorder(name, share),
                          group = factor(group, levels = c("white", "black", "hispanic"),
                                         labels = c("white", "Black", "Hispanic")))

tinyplot::tinytheme("minimal")
tinyplot::tinyplot(share ~ name | group, data = by_name_sorted, type = "barplot", flip = TRUE,
                   palette = c("grey60", "#4a78ab", "#8b1538"),
                   legend = list(title = "Names meant to indicate"),
                   xlab = NA, ylab = "Replies that greeted the sender by name (%)")
tinyplot::tinytheme()
```

`palette` gives one colour for each group, in the order of the levels of the factor, which is why the groups are made a factor first, with the labels that the legend should show. `legend` sets the title of the legend. `xlab` and `ylab` supply the words on the axes; with `flip = TRUE`, `xlab` still belongs to the column after the tilde, now drawn vertically, and `NA` leaves it blank. `tinytheme("minimal")` sets the look of everything that carries no data, the gridlines, the frame and the type, until `tinytheme()` without an argument restores the default.

A third column can also split a figure into panels with shared axes, which are called **facets**. The chart below compares the female and the male names of each group, with `facet = ~name_sex`. Make the column of the facets a factor first, so that each panel is headed by its label:

```{r}
#| label: fig-tinyplot-facets
#| fig-cap: "The share of replies that greeted the sender by name, by the group of the name, for the female and the male names. Source: `cases/housing/data/housing_audit.csv`."
#| fig-height: 3
by_sex <- audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named)) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(share = 100 * mean(named), by = c("group", "name_sex")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(name_sex = factor(name_sex, labels = c("female names", "male names")))

tinyplot::tinyplot(share ~ group, facet = ~name_sex, data = by_sex, type = "barplot",
                   xlab = NA, ylab = "Greeted by name (%)")
```

Both Hispanic names drew fewer greetings than the names of the other two groups, and the gap is larger for the male name, Santiago, than for the female one, Gabriela. A tinyplot is drawn straight onto the plotting device and is not stored as an object, so a figure is written to a file by opening the file first, with `png("names.png", width = 7, height = 4, units = "in", res = 300)`, drawing, and closing the file with `dev.off()`.

Every figure so far reduces a yes-or-no outcome to a share, one number for each name or group. A measure that can take many values, such as a length of time, is better drawn whole, so that the reader can judge its spread and its shape as well as its centre, and the usual figure for a single measure of this kind is a histogram, which divides the range of the measure into intervals, called bins, and draws a bar for the number of cases in each. The housing-audit data hold one such measure, the length of the wait list that a reply gave, in months. It is stored as text in `waitlist`, because some replies gave words rather than numbers, `Closed` or `No Housing`, so the first step keeps the entries that are numbers and converts them. `grepl("^[0-9.]+$", waitlist)` is `TRUE` for an entry made only of digits and decimal points, and `FALSE` for a word or a missing value.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tinyplot-waits
#| fig-cap: "The length of the wait list given in the replies that stated one in months, in bins of three months. Source: `cases/housing/data/housing_audit.csv`."
#| fig-alt: "Histogram of wait lists from 0 to 120 months. Most lie below two years, with tall bars at 6 and 12 months, smaller peaks at 24 and 36 months, and two long waits beyond five years."
#| fig-height: 3.2
waits <- audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(grepl("^[0-9.]+$", waitlist)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(months = as.numeric(waitlist))

tinyplot::tinyplot(~ months, data = waits, type = tinyplot::type_histogram(breaks = seq(0, 120, by = 3)),
                   xlab = "Wait list given in the reply (months)", ylab = "Replies")
```

A formula with nothing before the tilde, `~ months`, asks for a single variable, and `type_histogram()` sets the edges of the bins with `breaks`, here every three months from 0 to 120. Of the `r nrow(waits)` replies that gave a number, half quoted a wait of between `r stats::quantile(waits$months, 0.25)` and `r stats::quantile(waits$months, 0.75)` months, around a median of `r stats::median(waits$months)` months, while a few quoted far longer waits, up to `r max(waits$months)` months, which is why the distribution has a long tail to the right and its mean, `r fmt(mean(waits$months))` months, lies above the median. The tall bars at 6 and 12 months and the smaller ones at 24 and 36 months most likely come from the round numbers in which officials speak of waits, and from the OAs, who converted phrases such as "two years" into months, so the measure is heaped at half-years and whole years. Adding `| group` to the formula colours the bars by the group of the name, and `facet = ~group` draws one histogram for each group, which is how the waits quoted to the three groups would be compared.

### ggplot2 {#sec-first-ggplot}

The ggplot2 package draws the figures of the pages and slides of this site. Its name abbreviates 'the grammar of graphics', the idea that any chart can be described as a combination of a few standard parts: the data, a mapping from columns to visual properties such as position and colour, and the shapes that are drawn, called geoms. Scales, labels and a theme finish the figure. A bar chart and a scatterplot are two fillings of the same parts, so once you know the parts you can read the code of any figure on this site.

A plot needs data, a mapping and at least one geom, and everything else has a default good enough to start with:

```{r}
#| label: fig-first
#| fig-cap: "The share of replies that greeted the sender by name, by name: the first draft."
#| fig-height: 3
ggplot2::ggplot(by_name, ggplot2::aes(x = share, y = name)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col()
```

`ggplot()` receives the data frame. `aes()` is the **aesthetic mapping**, which says that the share governs the horizontal position and the name the vertical position. `geom_col()` draws one bar per row, with a length equal to the value in the data. Its cousin `geom_bar()` counts the rows for you instead, and reaching for the wrong one of the two is a frequent small frustration. Layers are joined with `+`, never with the pipe: ggplot2 settled on `+` years before R had a native pipe, and typing `|>` where `+` belongs is among the commonest errors of the first week.

The bars come out in alphabetical order and in one colour. The same two changes make the figure readable. `reorder(name, share)` sorts the names by the value being plotted, and `fill = group` inside `aes()` **maps** the colour of each bar to the group of its name, so that ggplot2 adds a legend explaining the colours. A property given outside `aes()`, such as `fill = "#0e3b6a"` in `geom_col()`, is **set** instead: one fixed value for every bar, with no legend because there is nothing to explain.

```{r}
#| label: fig-names
#| fig-cap: "The share of replies that greeted the sender by name, by the name that signed the email. Source: `cases/housing/data/housing_audit.csv`."
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of six names. Emily, Brett and Tyrone lie near 60%, Shanice near 52%, Gabriela near 46% and Santiago near 37%; the bars of the two Hispanic names are burgundy."
#| fig-height: 3.4
ggplot2::ggplot(by_name, ggplot2::aes(x = share, y = reorder(name, share), fill = group)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(white = "grey60", black = "#4a78ab", hispanic = "#8b1538"),
    labels = c(white = "white", black = "Black", hispanic = "Hispanic"),
    name   = "Names meant to indicate"
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Replies that greeted the sender by name (%)", y = NULL) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

The **scale** decides which colours the mapping uses. `scale_fill_manual()` names a colour for each group, and giving `values` and `labels` as named vectors, with `white = …` rather than a bare list of colours, means that the assignment cannot reverse itself if the groups arrive in another order. `labs()` supplies the words, which deserve more care than beginners give them, because a column name such as `share` means nothing to a reader who has not opened the codebook. `theme_minimal()` sets the look of everything that carries no data, and its `base_size` scales all the type at once.

Read the figure as the claim of the case. Both Hispanic names drew fewer greetings by name than any other name, and the two names that were meant to indicate each group do not always agree, which is why the design used a male and a female name for every group. Unlike a tinyplot, a ggplot2 plot is an ordinary R object, so it can be stored under a name and written to a file with `ggplot2::ggsave("names.png", p, width = 7, height = 4)`, which takes its dimensions in inches.

Two arguments of the wider grammar are worth knowing from the start. Line thickness is set with `linewidth`, whereas the size of a point or of a piece of type is set with `size`, because `size` on a point means an area and on text a height, neither of which is a line thickness. Passing `size` to a line geom still works, but R warns that this use was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0. To look more closely at part of a figure, zoom with `coord_cartesian()` rather than with the `limits` argument of a scale. A scale with `limits` removes every row outside the range before any statistic is computed, so that a fitted line is refitted on whatever rows remain, while `coord_cartesian()` zooms the finished figure and leaves the computation untouched.

Where two figures belong side by side, the **patchwork** package composes whole plots. `patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2)` sets two plot objects in a row, and `patchwork::wrap_plots(plots, nrow = 1)` does the same for a list of them.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Add `ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(label = round(share, 1)), hjust = -0.2)` to the last figure, so that each bar carries its value. Then move `fill = group` out of `aes()` and into `geom_col()`, read the error that it raises, and replace it with `fill = "#0e3b6a"`, a colour set rather than mapped. Finally, add `ggplot2::facet_wrap(ggplot2::vars(group))` and decide whether three small panels say more than one chart does. In tinyplot, the same three changes are `type = "text"` with `labels = round(by_name$share, 1)`, `col = "#0e3b6a"` in place of the vertical bar in the formula, and `facet = ~group`.
:::

## 13. A first look at `try_spec()` {#sec-try-spec}

The workspace holds a file of helper functions, `R/spec_tools.R`, which the exercise loads once and then uses to fit specifications. A **specification** is one complete set of choices for an analysis: which names are compared, which emails are counted, what happens to the uncoded replies, which model is fitted and which covariates it holds. `source()` runs the file, so that its functions become available in your session. In the browser lab the helpers are already loaded, and the line is not needed.

```{r}
#| label: source-tools
#| eval: false
source("R/spec_tools.R")
```

```{r}
#| label: source-tools-page
#| include: false
# The page reads the helpers from the copy of the workspace beside the site,
# the nested repository in _workspaces/housing/, and its data/ from the folder
# of the case, which holds the same files.
source("../../_workspaces/housing/R/spec_tools.R")
```

`try_spec()` fits one specification and prints its result. Every argument has a default, and the defaults are the reference specification of [section 10](#sec-shares), so calling the function with no arguments reproduces the gap that you computed by hand:

```{r}
#| label: try-reference
try_spec()
```

The first lines repeat the two shares and their difference, `r fmt(ref_row$b_pp, 2)` points, now with a 95% interval around it. The test line comes from a linear probability model, a regression of the 0/1 outcome on an indicator of the Hispanic names, whose coefficient is exactly the difference in shares; the [binary-outcomes module](binary-outcomes.qmd) explains it. The last lines give the number of replies analysed, a partial correlation computed by the rule of the Multi100 project, the class of the result, and its place among the `r nrow(page_curve)` specifications of the curve of the claim.

Changing one argument changes one decision. `population = "all"` counts every delivered email, as the second calculation of section 10 did:

```{r}
#| label: try-all
try_spec(population = "all")
```

Options that are not on the curve are refused, with the reason why and the page of the course site that teaches them. Here the outcome is set to any reply rather than a greeting by name, which would answer a different claim:

```{r}
#| label: try-refused
#| error: true
try_spec(outcome = "reply")
```

Every call to `try_spec()` is logged, and `my_experiments()` prints the log, showing only the decisions that you varied:

```{r}
#| label: my-experiments
my_experiments()
```

That is the whole of Task 4 in miniature: change one decision at a time, read what moves, and keep a record. The [exercise overview](../cases/housing/exercise.qmd) sets out the five tasks, the [specification menu](../cases/housing/menu.qmd) lists every argument and its options, and the [cheatsheet](../cases/housing/cheatsheet.qmd) puts the helpers on one page. The rest of the course repeats the sequence that you have just practised on a small scale: read the data, look at it, reshape it with a few verbs, compute and draw, then fit and read what the fit says.

## 14. Other formats, and fetching data {#sec-formats}

The course file is a CSV, but the data reached the course as a file in the format of Stata (`.dta`), which the OAs deposited on the Harvard Dataverse. The [data sources module](data-sources.qmd#sec-dataverse) shows how to download it, by hand or through the API of the Dataverse, and [the next subsection](#sec-fetching) names the package that does it in R. R reads Stata files, and SPSS files (`.sav`), through the haven package, one function for each format:

```{r}
#| label: read-dta
#| eval: false
deposit <- haven::read_dta("HousingAuditAJPSFinalPublic_Unidentified.dta")   # haven::read_sav() reads SPSS
```

```{r}
#| label: read-dta-page
#| include: false
# The page reads the copy of the deposited file that the course keeps in
# data-raw/housing/, byte for byte the file on the Dataverse.
deposit <- haven::read_dta("../../data-raw/housing/dataverse_1HOVTU/HousingAuditAJPSFinalPublic_Unidentified.dta")
```

These formats differ from a CSV in storing **labelled data**. Each column can carry a variable label, a short description of what it holds, and a column of numeric codes can carry value labels, the words for which the codes stand. haven keeps both. In the deposited file, `poverty_pop_third` places the community of each housing authority in a third of the poverty rate, coded 1, 2 and 3, and it prints with its variable label and its value labels:

```{r}
#| label: labelled
head(deposit$poverty_pop_third)
```

`as_label()` from the sjlabelled package turns the codes into their labels, which gives a factor. It leaves out the labels of codes that no row holds, which `as_factor()` from haven would keep as empty levels. The row headed `NA` counts the emails whose community has no poverty third in the file:

```{r}
#| label: as-label
deposit$poverty_pop_third |>
  sjlabelled::as_label() |>
  datawizard::data_tabulate()
```

Labels are metadata that somebody typed, and they can be wrong. `get_label()` from sjlabelled returns the variable labels of the columns that it is given:

```{r}
#| label: label-error
deposit |>
  datawizard::data_select(select = c("HardEmail", "HispanicEmailer")) |>
  sjlabelled::get_label()
```

`HispanicEmailer` records whether the official who replied had a Hispanic name, the column `hispanic_official` of the course file, and yet it carries the same label as the column before it, the hard-to-find address. The codebook that the OAs deposited beside the file labels it "Respondent had Hispanic name", and the [codebook of the public file](../cases/housing/data/audit_original_codebook.md) records the slip. Read the labels as a first guide and the codebook as the authority.

Many organisations keep their data in **Excel** files, and the `readxl` package reads them one sheet at a time, since a workbook is really a stack of tables. The file names in this block and the next are illustrative, since the course ships no workbook and no Parquet file:

```r
rates <- readxl::read_excel("unemployment_rates.xlsx", sheet = "annual")
```

Treat what arrives from a spreadsheet with mild suspicion. Excel displays one thing and stores another often enough – dates especially – that column types should be checked with `summary()` straight after every import.

Finally, **Parquet** and **Feather** are the newer columnar formats, which store a table column by column, and you will increasingly meet them where datasets are large or move between programming languages. They are compressed and fast, and unlike a CSV they store the type of each column inside the file, so nothing has to be re-inferred on reading. The `arrow` package reads both, and the small `nanoparquet` package reads and writes Parquet without needing any other package:

```r
emails <- arrow::read_parquet("housing_audit.parquet")   # arrow::read_feather() for Feather
```

Whatever the source format, what you end up with in R is the same data frame, and everything downstream – the verbs of sections 8 and 9, the models fitted in later modules – proceeds identically. Every `read_` function here also has a `write_` counterpart (`write_csv()`, `write_dta()`, `write_parquet()`, and `write_xlsx()` from the `writexl` package), so R also serves as the converter between all of these formats. The course ships its data as CSV all the same, because for tables of a few hundred or a thousand rows the efficiency of the binary formats buys nothing, while plain text can be opened in anything, compared line by line or read in an email.

### Fetching data from a repository or an API {#sec-fetching}

Most data come from an archive, a statistical office or a repository, and for many of those sources an R package fetches the data straight into a data frame. The query is then written down in your script instead of being clicked through on a website, and that is what makes the download repeatable. The [data sources module](data-sources.qmd) maps the sources and works through the route of the housing-audit file step by step, while this subsection covers the packages that query them, which fall into three groups.

**Repositories of deposited work**, which need no account for a public file. The `dataverse` package downloads a file from any Dataverse installation by the DOI of its record, which is how the [data sources module](data-sources.qmd#sec-dataverse) fetches the deposited file that this section read:

```r
deposit <- dataverse::get_dataframe_by_name(
  "HousingAuditAJPSFinalPublic_Unidentified.tab",
  dataset  = "doi:10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU",
  server   = "dataverse.harvard.edu",
  original = TRUE,             # the Stata file as deposited, not the tab-separated copy
  .f       = haven::read_dta   # the function that reads it
)
```

`osfr` reads and writes the Open Science Framework through its API, and `zen4R` does the same for Zenodo, and deposits there as well. For a source with no package, `httr2` sends the request and `jsonlite` parses the answer, and `rvest` reads a table out of a web page, with the caution that scraping a site is subject to its terms and to the courtesy of not hammering it.

**Indicators from the international organisations and statistical offices**, which are open and need no account. The `WDI` package (and `wbstats`, which covers more of the World Bank databases) queries the World Bank indicators by their codes:

```r
macro <- WDI::WDI(country = c("DE", "FR", "GB"),
                  indicator = c(unemp = "SL.UEM.TOTL.NE.ZS", growth = "NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG"),
                  start = 2004, end = 2013)
```

The `eurostat` package does the same for the Eurostat tables (`get_eurostat("une_rt_a")` fetches the annual unemployment table, with `restatapi` as an alternative that uses the newer API, the interface through which programs request data from Eurostat); `OECD` and the general-purpose `rsdmx` query the OECD and any other service that publishes in SDMX, the standard format in which many statistical agencies exchange data; `Rilostat` reaches ILOSTAT; `onsr` the Office for National Statistics; `wid` the World Inequality Database. Each returns a long, tidy table, one row per country and period, that pivots into whatever shape a model needs.

**Survey and census microdata behind a registration.** Packages are fewer here, and less dependable, because an archive that asks for an account and a statement of purpose seldom offers programs a way in. Where one does, the credentials belong in an environment variable or a keyring, never in the script. `ipumsr` builds and downloads IPUMS extracts through the IPUMS API and reads them with their labels. The ESS Data Portal has a download API of its own, still in beta, while the `essurvey` package was written for the download site that the ESS replaced on 30 May 2022 and has had no release since. The GESIS archive offers no such interface. The `gesisdata` package scripts the clicks of a download by driving a web browser, but it has not been updated since July 2023, and a report of a failed download, opened on its issue tracker in February 2025, has had no answer. `rdhs` serves the Demographic and Health Surveys, `pewdata` the files of the Pew Research Center, and `manifestoR` the coded programmes of the Manifesto Project with an API key, and any such package is worth testing on one file before a project is built on it. Whatever the package, the file that arrives is usually Stata or SPSS, and haven reads it with its labels, as the first part of this section showed.

Two habits keep a fetched dataset reproducible. Write the fetch as a function or a script of its own, save what it returns as a dated file, and read that file in the analysis, so that the analysis does not depend on the network being up or the source being unchanged. And record the version or the download date in the file name or the README, because the World Bank and Eurostat revise past years without renaming the series.

## 15. Three dialects {#sec-dialects}

R is old enough to have grown dialects, families of packages with their own vocabulary and style, all doing the same underlying work. You will meet three – base R, the tidyverse and easystats – and this section sets the same small task in each, so that none of them ever looks foreign. The task is to keep the delivered emails, the ones with a reply status, with four of their columns.

**Base R** does it with the bracket-and-`$` machinery of [section 4](#sec-dataframes), no packages required:

```{r}
#| label: dialect-base
delivered <- audit[!is.na(audit$reply), c("name", "group", "reply", "named")]  # r-style: keep – base R, shown for comparison
nrow(delivered)
```

It works, and code written this way twenty years ago still runs. Its weakness is that the brackets spell out the mechanics of the selection, so the reader must decode positions and conditions to reconstruct what the line is for.

**The tidyverse** is the dominant modern dialect, a family of packages that share one design philosophy and can be installed and attached under the single name `tidyverse` [@WickhamEtAl2019WelcomeTidyverse]. You have already met two of its members, readr, whose `read_csv()` section 6 used, and dplyr, whose `if_else()` and `transmute()` sections 10 and 11 used. In dplyr, the same task reads as a list of named steps:

```{r}
#| label: dialect-dplyr
delivered <- audit |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(reply)) |>            # the delivered emails only
  dplyr::select(name, group, reply, named)   # the columns of interest
nrow(delivered)
```

`dplyr::mutate()` derives a new column from existing ones, and `dplyr::summarise()` reduces the table to a single row, or, after `dplyr::group_by()`, to one row per group. The chain below keeps the delivered emails, adds the greeting counted among all of them, as the second calculation of [section 10](#sec-shares) did, groups the emails by the group of the name, and reports three numbers for each group:

```{r}
#| label: dialect-dplyr-summary
audit |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(reply)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(greeted = dplyr::if_else(reply == 1, named, 0)) |>   # no reply counts as no greeting
  dplyr::group_by(group) |>                                         # one set of rows per group of names
  dplyr::summarise(
    emails     = dplyr::n(),                    # how many delivered emails
    reply_rate = mean(reply),                   # the share that drew a reply
    greeted    = mean(greeted, na.rm = TRUE)    # the share greeted by name, the five uncoded replies left out
  )
```

Read the chain aloud and it is almost English: take the emails, keep the delivered ones, add a column for the greeting, group by the names, and for each group report the count and two shares. Readability of that kind serves reproducibility, because a reviewer who can read the code can check it, and that is why the scripts of the course are built from chains of named verbs.

**easystats** is the third dialect, and the one that the course reaches for first. It is likewise a family of packages under one installable name, `easystats` [@LudeckeEtAl2022EasystatsFrameworkEasy]. Its data-preparation member is datawizard, the package of sections 7 to 11, whose verbs are modelled on those of dplyr, and the course uses it wherever it has the verb that a task needs, before turning to dplyr:

```{r}
#| label: dialect-datawizard
delivered <- audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(reply)) |>
  datawizard::data_select(select = c("name", "group", "reply", "named"))
nrow(delivered)
```

The other members are built for what happens *after* a model is fitted, the subject of [section 16](#sec-easystats). The three dialects are used together, in layers. Base R is always underneath, datawizard and the tidyverse give data work a grammar of named verbs, and the rest of easystats gives the modelling stage one of its own.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Write a chain on `audit` that keeps only the emails signed Santiago (`datawizard::data_filter(name == "Santiago")`), selects `reply` and `named`, and prints the result. Then extend it with `datawizard::data_summary()` to report the share of the emails to Santiago that drew a reply, leaving out the bounced ones with `mean(reply, na.rm = TRUE)`. If you are curious, redo the first step in base R and in dplyr, and notice that you can already read all three.
:::

## 16. Naming the estimand {#sec-easystats}

Fitting models is the subject of the methods modules. On these data, the [binary-outcomes module](binary-outcomes.qmd) builds from the table of counts of section 10 up to the logistic regression of the paper. Nothing that follows is needed for the tasks. It is here because it completes the map of the dialects, and because it ties the tools of R to the habit that the course asks of you throughout, which is to name the quantity you want before you estimate it.

Take the simplest model of the claim, a linear model of the greeting on the group of the name, fitted to the replies that carry a greeting code. With an outcome of 0s and 1s and a predictor made of groups, each coefficient is a difference between two shares, the quantity of [section 10](#sec-shares). One step comes first. The modelbased package used below works through the marginaleffects package, which refuses a column called `group` because its own output has a column of that name, so the column is renamed, and made a factor with the white names first, before the model is fitted:

```{r}
#| label: lm-groups
replies <- audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named)) |>
  datawizard::data_rename(select = "group", replacement = "names_of") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(names_of = factor(names_of, levels = c("white", "black", "hispanic")))

m <- lm(named ~ names_of, data = replies)
```

In base R you call `summary(m)` and read the printout. The easystats packages instead give you one function for each question you might ask of the fitted model:

```{r}
#| label: easystats-model
parameters::model_parameters(m)     # the coefficient table as a data frame, with confidence intervals
performance::model_performance(m)   # fit indices, R2, AIC and the like, in one row
```

```{r}
#| label: easystats-more
#| eval: false
performance::check_model(m)         # the diagnostic checks in one figure: residuals, influential rows
report::report(m)                   # the model written out in sentences
```

`model_parameters()` returns the coefficients as a data frame that you can filter, join or plot [@LudeckeEtAl2020ExtractingComputingExploring]. The row `names of [hispanic]`, in which the function has written the name of the column in words, is the gap between the Hispanic and the white names, on the scale of a share rather than in percentage points. `check_model()` draws the standard diagnostic checks in one figure [@LudeckeEtAl2021PerformanceRPackage], and `report()` writes the results paragraph itself, with the numbers drawn live from the object. Its words are generic, though. It calls each coefficient an effect, a word that a comparison among replies earns only under the assumptions that the [audit-experiments module](experiments.qmd#sec-posttreatment) sets out, and a sentence written for any model needs editing before it describes this one. In a rendered Quarto document the numbers in such prose cannot fall out of step with the model, as a number pasted in by hand can.

One member of the family, `modelbased`, builds the habit of naming the quantity into its functions [@MakowskiEtAl2025ModelbasedRPackage]. The coefficients in a table are whatever quantities the parameterisation of the model happens to produce, so that a different reference group would give different coefficients from the same fit. These functions make you *name the quantity you want* – the **estimand** – and then compute that quantity from the model:

```{r}
#| label: modelbased
modelbased::estimate_means(m, by = "names_of")             # the expected share greeted by name, for each group of names
modelbased::estimate_contrasts(m, contrast = "names_of")   # the differences between those shares
```

The expected outcome under each condition and the contrast between two conditions are each a quantity that you can state in words before touching the software, and the contrast of the Hispanic with the white names is the gap of section 10 once more. Under the bonnet these functions call the `marginaleffects` package, which does the job that Stata users will know from `margins`. The intervals above rest on the ordinary standard errors of a linear model, which assume that the outcome varies as much in every group. `try_spec()` uses HC2 standard errors, which allow the variance of a 0/1 outcome to differ from group to group, and `estimate_contrasts(m, contrast = "names_of", vcov = "HC2")` asks for them here. Saying what you want to estimate first, and only then deriving the analysis that estimates it, is what the course practises in Task 2, with the estimand statement and the causal graph, and again in Task 5, where you state your specification and the quantity that it estimates in the preregistration block of your report before running it.

## Sources and further study {#sec-sources}

This module was written for the course and adapts no existing lesson, so there is no borrowed text to attribute. It teaches only the part of R that the materials of the course use, in the order in which the course needs it, together with the map of dialects that puts those materials in context.

For a fuller, self-paced grounding in R, these open resources are recommended:

- **The Carpentries, "R for Reproducible Scientific Analysis" and "Programming with R".** <https://swcarpentry.github.io/r-novice-gapminder/> and <https://swcarpentry.github.io/r-novice-inflammation/>. Licensed CC BY 4.0, and the standard hands-on introductions to R for researchers, covering objects, vectors and data frames in far more depth than this page.
- **The Turing Way, "Guide for Reproducible Research".** <https://book.the-turing-way.org/>. Licensed CC BY 4.0. Not an R tutorial as such, but the best short statement of why the habits that this module practises – scripts over console history, relative paths, one file for analysis and report – are worth building from the first day.
- **"R for Data Science"**, the free book by the authors of the tidyverse packages, at <https://r4ds.hadley.nz/>. Its chapters on data transformation and on visualisation cover the dplyr counterparts of the verbs of section 9 and the grammar of ggplot2 of section 12 in full.
- **The documentation of the packages**, which is readable as an introduction as well as a reference: [easystats.github.io/datawizard](https://easystats.github.io/datawizard/), [grantmcdermott.com/tinyplot](https://grantmcdermott.com/tinyplot/), [dplyr.tidyverse.org](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/), [readr.tidyverse.org](https://readr.tidyverse.org/), [ggplot2.tidyverse.org](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/), [vincentarelbundock.github.io/tinytable](https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/tinytable/), [easystats.github.io/easystats](https://easystats.github.io/easystats/), [haven.tidyverse.org](https://haven.tidyverse.org/), [readxl.tidyverse.org](https://readxl.tidyverse.org/), and the arrow R package site at [arrow.apache.org/docs/r](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/r/).

When you are ready for a first statistical model, the [binary-outcomes module](binary-outcomes.qmd) starts from the table of counts of section 10 and builds up to the logistic regression of the housing-audit paper.
